recordings.text: The fork, a pattern every player must learn: a single piece attacks several targets, and the defender can rescue only one of them.
The fork serves either side of the board. This move lets the other side set one up, with a single piece reaching for several targets at once.
A fork was on offer in another move: one piece, several targets, and only one of them able to escape. The played move lets that pattern pass.
Here is the pin to the king, a pattern worth knowing by heart. The pinned piece must stay on its line, because stepping aside would expose its own king.
A pin binds a piece to the king behind it. This move lets the other side apply one, and the pinned piece would then be held on its line.
A pin to the king was available in another move. A piece held that way must stay on its line or expose its own king, and the played move forgoes it.
The skewer is the pin turned around. The valuable piece stands in front; when it steps aside, the piece behind it is laid open.
Beware the skewer, the pin's reversed cousin. This gives the other side one: the front piece may have to move and leave the piece behind it exposed.
The skewer belonged to a stronger move. Strike the front piece, and once it steps away, the piece standing behind it is exposed. The pattern was there to use.
An old principle: to win what is guarded, remove the guard. This move captures a defender, so study what that defender was protecting.
What is guarded is only as safe as its guard. This lets the other side capture a defender, and whatever it protected could then stand without cover.
Another move could have removed a defender by capture, leaving whatever it guarded without protection. A reliable method, and it was available.
The back-rank mate is among the most reliable patterns there is. The king's own pieces wall it in, and an attacker on the last rank finishes the work.
Mark this pattern well: the back-rank mate. After this move the other side has a route to it, because the king's own pieces hem it in.
A back-rank mate was within reach, the king boxed in by its own guards. This move lets that well-known finish slip away.
Every pawn carries the possibility of a queen. The idea here is promotion, so follow the pawn's road to the last rank.
A pawn near the last rank deserves constant attention. After this move, one of the other side's pawns has a path to promotion; trace the pawn that could make the journey.
A stronger move opened the road to promotion for a pawn. This move leaves that pawn short of the last rank, and the chance passes.
The discovered attack is a fine device. One piece steps out of the way, and the piece behind it strikes along the line it uncovers.
A piece standing in front of another can hide a threat. This hands the other side a discovered attack, where the front piece steps away and the piece behind it strikes.
A discovered attack lay in another move. The front piece would have stepped aside, opening the line behind it to a threat. The device stayed unused.
Two threats at once is a sound principle, and a single reply rarely answers both. This move makes the double attack.
A position that allows two threats at once is hard to defend. This move gives the other side a double attack; find both threats before choosing an answer.
Two threats at once were available through a stronger move. This one passes over that double attack, and with it the hardest kind of problem for a defender.
Deflection rests on a simple truth: a defender cannot guard a post it has been lured away from. This move draws one off, and its duty is left unattended.
A defender with an important duty can be lured away. This move gives the other side that deflection, so mark what the defender is holding now.
A defender could have been lured from its post by another move. No one reached for that deflection; study what the defender had to hold.
The simplest principle of all still applies, and an unguarded piece falls to the first attacker. Here this move takes one. Before any combination, count the loose pieces.
An unguarded piece was there to collect with another move, and the played move passes it by. Loose pieces should be counted before anything more elaborate.
Pieces without a guard invite capture. This move leaves one for the other side to take; look for the piece that has lost its protection.
A defender has a duty before it has a destination. Here the only real defender of a piece walks away, and the other side can now capture what was left unguarded.
Every move asks a question, and the opponent's last one created a threat. This move leaves it unanswered, so a piece can now be captured.
An exchange is judged after the recapture, not before. Here the first capture is answered by the loss of a more valuable piece.
Development is the first principle of the opening. This brings a minor piece off its home square; note where it now stands.
Another move would have developed a minor piece from its home square. The opening rewards each piece that joins the game.
Rooks belong on open files; that is one of the steadiest rules we have. This rook now has such a file, free of pawns of both colors.
Another move would have given a rook an open file, with not a pawn of either color upon it. Rooks are at their best on such roads.
A semi-open file is the next best thing for a rook. This rook has no friendly pawns on its file, though at least one enemy pawn remains.
Another move would have given a rook a semi-open file, free of its own pawns, with an enemy pawn still standing there.
A passed pawn is a lasting asset. This leaves one, with its own file and both neighboring files free of enemy pawns ahead of it.
Another move would have produced a passed pawn, one with no enemy pawn ahead of it on its own file or on either side.
Passed pawns must be pushed, as the old saying has it. This one was already passed, and the move carries it further forward.
Another move would have carried the passed pawn further along its road. Compare where it could have stood with where it stays.
An isolated pawn has no neighbor to lean on. This move leaves one, with no friendly pawn on either adjacent file.
Another move would have left an isolated pawn, without a friendly pawn on either neighboring file.
A guarded piece is a calm piece. This move gives a piece the defender it lacked.
Another move would have given an unguarded piece a defender, so it would no longer stand alone.
One piece is left to stand alone after this move, with no defender at all. An undefended piece is a weakness, but not yet proof that it can be won.
Had another move been played, a piece would have stood unguarded. By itself, that would not prove the piece could be won.
A king with an escape square is harder to trap. This move opens a legal flight square that was not there before; compare the positions to see what cleared it.
With another move, the king would have gained a legal square of retreat. Compare the two positions to find what would have cleared the way.
Castling serves two purposes at once. The king steps toward shelter, and the rook comes toward the center.
The other path was castling, with the king toward shelter, the rook toward the center, both in a single turn.
The two bishops together cover every square color, and that partnership is often valued. This capture ends the bishop pair for the side that loses the bishop.
Another move would have taken a bishop and ended the opposing side's partnership of two bishops.
Doubled pawns are a familiar structural weakness. Here one pawn now stands directly in front of another of its own color.
Another move would have left doubled pawns, one pawn standing in front of a second of the same color.
The king's safety outranks every other lesson. Here the move permits a forced checkmate; trace the attack to the point where the defense gives way.
Checkmate could have been forced with another move, and the played move lets that mate escape. Return to the position; it is worth finding and remembering.
Some dangers arrive all at once. This move places checkmate in the other side's hands for their very next move.
A forced mate is a path with no turnings. This move sets out on it, and every defense ends at checkmate, though further down the way.
A forced mate, once begun, must be carried through. This move keeps it on course, though the finish is not yet here.
The mate remains forced, and the ending will not change. Still, a shorter road to it existed in another move; that road is worth knowing.
The final step is set. Whatever answer comes, the side that moved will checkmate with its next move.
For the side that just moved, the mate was already sealed. This move hastens the end; a sterner defense would have held it at bay longer.
When the mate cannot be stopped, the old discipline is to make it travel the longest road. This move takes a road as long as any the search found.
A sacrifice is tested by its acceptance. Here the offered material can be taken, and the idea still holds in the line that was checked.
Some positions offer a single narrow path. Of the moves examined, this alone kept the position playable, while every alternative lost.
This move is the one thread that kept the advantage; every alternative examined would have lost. The whole position rested on it.
Look first at what the reply can take. The other side has a capture available at once.
A check must be answered before all else. The strongest reply gives check, so the king's safety comes first.
The engine has a different move in mind here. Set the two side by side on the board and compare what the replies allow.
By the engine's measure, this falls short of the best option. Study the reply, for that is where the cost first appears.
Among the moves the engine examined, this is a strong choice. A choice the position bears out.
Sound, by any fair measure. The engine has another preference, yet this keeps most of what the position offered.
This move stands in a recognized opening line, a road many games have traveled before.
Here the game steps past the last move our opening book recognizes. From this point, the position must be read on its own terms.
The earlier setback is answered here, and the position is playable once more. A setback need not be the end of the lesson.
The earlier setback is repaired, and play is possible again. The other side's errors had a hand in that recovery.
A gift must be seen before it can be taken. The opponent's last move offered one, and this move accepts it.
An opportunity arrived with the opponent's last move, and the reply here leaves it untaken. The stronger answer is one move back, waiting to be found.
When a pattern repeats, the repetition is itself the lesson. This issue showed up earlier in the reviewed game as well; set the examples side by side and find the warning sign they share.
Protection has returned to a piece that was left unguarded earlier. Set the two positions side by side and see what restored it.
Small concessions accumulate quietly. This move is one of several that have worn the position down together, so study the sequence rather than this move alone.
Converting an advantage asks for its own discipline. From here to the recorded win the advantage never slipped; trace that stretch move by move.
Your other saved games show this same issue. A pattern seen in several games is a pattern worth studying across all of them.
Checkmate. The king has no legal escape, and the attack is complete. Keep this finish in memory.
Checkmate. Every legal square is closed to the king, and the lesson lies earlier, in the moment the defense could still have held.
A drawn game. Neither side could force more, and the turning points are still worth study.
Study the position before you act, and only then decide on a move.
That attempt does not survive the reply. Return to the position and look for the pattern it contains.
That attempt went unanswered. Play the move again, and we shall see.
For the side that made this move, the saved engine analysis holds a forced checkmate.
By the saved engine analysis, this move opens the way to a forced checkmate for the other side.
Weigh the material once the saved line is over. Against the starting position, the side that made this move has come out with more.
Weigh the material once the saved line is over. Against the starting position, the side that made this move has come out with less.
The exercise takes this move as an answer, yet the moves shown hold no clear tactical explanation. I will not invent one.
The exercise does not accept this move, and the moves shown give no clear tactical reason. Study the position again with fresh eyes.
One of the saved answers, matched exactly. In this exercise, the saved answers are the measure.
This move is not among the exercise's saved answers. That alone does not make another legal move poor chess.
Give the move careful study before the next position.
Good. Keep its reason alongside it; the reason is what returns when the pattern does.
Your practice has been saved, and your review dates have not moved.
Solved. Even so, this recall keeps its relearning mark.
Our study begins from this position, before any of the moves are played.
The next move in the line. Mark the change it makes.
Check. The king is attacked, and every other concern must wait.
Here the king escapes the check.
Its journey complete, the pawn arrives on the last rank and is promoted.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and the new piece gives check.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and the result is checkmate, with the king left no legal way out.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and the move also lifts the check on its own king.
With this move, a piece leaves the board by capture.
This captures a piece, and the same move gives check.
This capture is also checkmate, leaving the king no legal square.
The capture also lifts the check from the king.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes in a single stroke.
The pawn captures its way onto the last rank and promotes, giving check with the new piece.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, and that is checkmate, with every legal square closed to the king.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, and in doing so it frees its own king from check.
Castling here does double work: king and rook take their new squares, and the move gives check.
Castling here ends the game: king and rook take their new squares, and the opposing king is checkmated, without a legal way out.
The fork, demonstrated: one piece attacks several targets and then takes one of them. By the example's end, the side that forked stands ahead by a net gain in material.
The pin to the king forbids this capture: the piece may not leave its line, because that would expose its own king.
Pinned to its king, the attacked piece has little freedom to escape. It may move only where the king stays shielded.
Pinned to their own king, the defenders are unable to recapture there. That is the reason the capture works, and the line shown ends with a gain in material.
Watch what becomes of the pinned piece. Bound to its line by the king behind it, it is captured before these moves are done.
The skewer, completed: the front piece leaves the line, and the piece it was shielding is taken along that same line.
The check compels the king to leave the line. The same attacker then collects whatever stood behind the king.
The lone defender falls first, and then the piece it guarded. Mark how the first capture makes the second possible.
The defender is lured from its post, and what it was guarding falls in its absence.
The blocker moves aside, and a line opens behind it. The piece on that line makes the capture.
A piece steps off the line, and the one behind it delivers check: the discovered check.
Double check: two pieces attack the king together, and only a king move can answer both.
The moving piece makes one attack and uncovers a second along the line it leaves. In the example, that second piece completes the capture.
The pawn reaches promotion, and in this example that side finishes with a net material gain as well.
An unguarded piece is captured here, and the side that takes it finishes the example with a net gain in material.
A relative pin held the attacking piece until the opponent's previous move released it. Left where it stood, the target falls in the line shown.
By the rules, the other side may answer with the marked reply. Set it on the board and study the position that results.
Before you move, survey your own pieces for any that could be taken without a useful recapture.
Before settling on a quiet move, survey the board for loose enemy pieces.
Examine the forcing moves for a single piece that can strike two valuable targets at once.
A pinned piece shields something behind it. Before moving one, see whether that is your king or a piece of greater value.
The first target is not always the whole story. Follow the line past it, to any valuable piece standing further back.
A defender's value includes everything it protects. Before exchanging one, see what depends on it.
A blocking piece hides a line; when it moves, study what that line opens.
Search for one move that creates two threats, and remember that checks and opened lines count among them.
Before a back-rank defender moves, make certain your king still has an escape square.
Count the steps a pawn needs to promote, and study the pawn advances that force a reply.
Before a defender moves, list every piece that relies on its protection.
Weigh what you capture against what the recapture takes back. The exchange is judged as a whole.
See whether a forcing exchange can lure a defender away from a second duty.
In this exercise, the saved answers are the authority. Another legal move is not made poor chess merely by their silence.
Here play unfolds against strong replies. Strong replies are not always forced ones.
Any material change belongs only to the line shown, measured from where that line begins. The piece values behind the count are listed in the written explanation.
No simple tactical reason emerges from the saved line, and I have inferred no positional one. Walk through it move by move and weigh the replies on your own.
The answer policy saved for this exercise governs the explanation, and its setting appears in the written notes.
The moves of the line you are studying, set out in order.
Correct; your chosen study material contains that move.

Play any move belonging to your selected opening lines; each is accepted.

That move lies outside your selected opening lines, so try once more. Retired positions keep their review schedules fixed, and this is one.
When you practice in mixed Due, this line supplies acceptable moves. Dedicated practice asks for this line and no other.
Your scheduled recalls will ask you to play your selected side's moves. A position held in common by several active studies uses a single card.
Please reload the saved session before you play another move.
The board now replays the verified line, move by move.
Revealed: that is how this attempt is recorded. Below, the solution may be replayed as often as you like.
After a retry, you found the full solution. Your record holds the earlier miss and the finish alike.
Every move of the solution found, with no misstep. Excellent work.
The puzzle is not solved by that move. Every correct move you made before it is still saved.
Correct; the puzzle continues. Now look for the move that follows.
Let calculation come before the hand moves. The pattern is there to be read.
I have too little from the engine to explain this position, and I will not guess at it.
Your review rests here for now. When you are ready, resume it below; until then, the pieces may be moved freely.
Select any move to study, or make a move on the board to test an idea.
A move recorded in the opening books. The position has its place in the literature.
The opening books record this move. We travel a well-trodden road.
A recognized opening move, already set down in the opening literature.
The opening literature still records this move.
The book continues; its pages have not run out yet.
The reply has its own place in the book.
A well-trodden road still; the opening record goes on.
Another move with an entry in the opening literature.
The book still keeps an entry for this one.
The recorded theory runs on through this move.
This move, too, appears in the book. Its place there is a matter of record, not a verdict on its quality.
Every game holds patterns worth learning. Let us read this one from its opening move.
I am Orin. The same patterns return across many games, and I have studied them a long while. Let us learn to recognize them in yours.
Every pattern I know, I first met over a board like this one. Let us play, and may a few of them find you here.
A sacrifice of rare quality. The material is spent, and the idea outlives the spending.
Few patterns are older than the sound sacrifice, and few are rarer. Here is one.
There is a kind of magic in giving up a piece and having it hold. Mark this one well.
Brilliant. Weighed in material alone, it costs; weighed in the searched line, the idea endures.
At the moment that mattered, a strong move. That is the oldest test, and it is passed here.
A great move. The position stood at a crossroads, and this move sets out on a strong road.
Great. A move is weighed by its hour as well as its merit, and this one weighs well on both.
Turning points are where games are decided. This one is met with strength.
The best move. The position posed a question, and this is its truest answer.
Precisely so. Nothing finer was to be found here.
Best. The discipline of the correct move is learned slowly and kept long.
Let us note it simply: the best move, and nothing to amend.
Good. A finer move existed, though the two are near neighbors in worth.
A good move. The very best lay a little further along, yet this path is a sound one.
Steadiness is its own virtue. A good move, and the position keeps its shape.
Not the keenest blade in the position, but a true one. Good.
A small inaccuracy. Precision lives in small choices, and this one strays a little.
Imprecise, though only slightly. A small tarnish on the position, nothing more.
An inaccuracy. A move may be nearly right and still not exact; this is such a move.
Here the position loosens, only a little. Small cracks are worth noting before they widen.
A real mistake. Errors of this size teach well, for those who return to study them.
Here the position pays a true price. This is an error worth remembering.
A clear error, of a kind as old as the game itself.
A mistake of real weight. What the position held a move ago, it holds less firmly now.
Opportunities in chess knock softly. One knocked here, and this move did not answer.
A chance went by. The position held a richer answer than the one given.
The board offered something here, and this move is spent on other business.
A missed chance. Let us remember the shape of this moment.
A blunder. In a single move, the scales of the position tip, and they tip far.
An error of the gravest order. Games turn on moves like this one.
Here fortune turns sharply. A blunder, and a heavy one.
A severe blunder. Of the lessons a game can hold, this is among the costliest.
That is not the move this chapter seeks. Consider the position afresh and choose again.
Just so; the chapter called for precisely that move. Let us continue.
Behold the move the chapter intended. Mark it well before proceeding.
Now the moves unfold of their own accord. Attend to each as it comes.
The moment is yours. Call forth what your study taught for this position.
We have turned aside onto a different road for a time. The main road awaits our return.
The chapter is complete, and your progress has been set down with care.
